Invasive red swamp crayfish detected for first time in Cass County, Michigan
The invasive red swamp crayfish has been found for the first time in Cass County's private pond near Niles. Authorities urge residents to report sightings as efforts continue statewide against further spread.
Invasive red swamp crayfish have been found in southwest Michigan’s Cass County for the first time, according to the Michigan Department of Natural Resources on Oct. 7. Two crayfish carcasses were discovered in a private pond near the city of Niles by the SW x SW Corner Cooperative Invasive Species Management Area during a snorkel survey for invasive aquatic plants in mid-September. The specimens were positively identified as invasive red swamp crayfish by staff from the Michigan Department of Natural Resources.
Red swamp crayfish are native to the southern United States but have been prohibited in Michigan since 2014 due to their high reproductive rate and ability to outcompete native species for food and habitat. They can be destructive to aquatic plants, leading to water quality issues, and their burrowing behavior can destabilize shorelines and infrastructure.
Populations of red swamp crayfish were first detected in Michigan in 2017, with initial discoveries at Sunset Lake in Kalamazoo and a retention pond in Novi. Since then, isolated infestations have been confirmed in Kalamazoo, Livingston, Macomb, Oakland, Van Buren and Wayne counties. Infestations are believed to result from aquarium pets being released or escaping, use as live bait, or live crayfish brought into Michigan for crawfish boils.
Residents of Berrien and Cass counties are asked to look for large crayfish (2 to 6 inches), generally brown to red with raised bumps on the body and claws. Red swamp crayfish also display an hourglass shape on their back that touches at the middle and a dark triangle visible on top of their tail. Specimens found should be collected if possible—bagged and frozen—or photographed closely from multiple angles with details noted about location, date, and time before reporting sightings to Kathleen Quebedeaux at DNR Fisheries Division.
Through collaboration among state agencies, local CISMAs (Cooperative Invasive Species Management Areas), universities including Michigan State University and Auburn University, U.S. Geological Survey, Gun Lake Tribe and others under the Michigan Invasive Species Program, efforts continue toward trapping methods and treatments aimed at limiting populations of this invasive species.
Because red swamp crayfish is prohibited under state law, it is illegal to knowingly possess or sell them alive; residents are urged not to release aquarium pets or plants into wild waters nor use bait outside its source location.
